sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Advancements in genome sequencing and genetic analysis technologies have significantly reduced the cost of sequenc-
ing and analyzing DNA. This has increased the accessibility and sharing of genomic data across various fields. In biotech-
nology, genomic data provides detailed genetic insights. In forensic sciences, genetic data is used extensively in criminal 
investigations. However, the widespread sharing of genomic data introduces substantial privacy and security concerns. 
Malicious individuals can exploit this data to identify individuals, leading to potential privacy breaches, identity tracing, 
extortion, or unauthorized surveillance [1 ].
Companies and research organizations often store genomic data in third-party cloud services. This increases the 
vulnerability of genomic data to cyber threats and unauthorized access. Such practices expose genomic datasets to 
re-identification, membership inference, and linkage attacks, often facilitated by public databases and social media

platforms [2]. Additionally, genomic data analysts frequently prioritize speed and accuracy over security. This approach 
increases the susceptibility of genomic software to vulnerabilities and cyber threats.
This review addresses the crucial balance between data utility and privacy. It systematically identifies key vulnerabili-
ties and evaluates privacy-preserving techniques used in genomic data [2 –4]. We discuss various technical solutions 
including data perturbation, cryptographic methods, and AI-driven defenses. The review also explores legal and ethical 
considerations to offer a comprehensive understanding of genomic privacy risks and protective measures. By reviewing 
current research and policy frameworks, we highlight existing gaps and suggest future research directions to improve 
genomic data security.
We categorize literature related to genomic privacy and security. The focus is on technical vulnerabilities, privacy-
preserving techniques, and regulatory frameworks. This review follows a structured literature review (SLR) approach. 
It includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, and regulatory guidelines. The goal is to ensure a com-
prehensive and up-to-date analysis. Our methodology involves selecting, analyzing, and evaluating relevant academic 
studies and policy documents. We apply inclusion and exclusion criteria to refine our selection process:
• Inclusion criteria: We include studies on novel security techniques, AI-driven privacy risks, cryptographic protec -
tions, and recent regulatory changes. We also prioritize research on comparative security frameworks, computational 
efficiency, and real-world applications.
• Exclusion criteria: We exclude studies that lack technical depth or focus only on ethical discussions without security 
solutions. We also remove outdated papers that do not cover recent AI-based genomic privacy risks. Studies that 
discuss general data privacy laws without relevance to genomics are not included.
We gather literature from IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar, ArXiv. We use a thematic categorization 
approach to structure the findings. The review is divided into genomic data attack types, cryptographic protections, AI-
driven threats, and regulatory frameworks. The goal is to highlight key trends, research gaps, and future directions. To 
maintain relevance, we focus on papers published between 2020 and 2025.
The paper is structured as follows: Section  2 discusses genomic data attacks; Section  3 reviews privacy-preserving 
methods; and Section 4 covers regulatory and ethical frameworks. Later sections critically evaluate computational effi-
ciency, AI-driven threats, and quantum-resistant solutions. The paper concludes by offering recommendations for future 
research directions.

sections.title: 2 Genomics data attacks
sections.text:
In this section, we categorize and explain various attacks on genomic data. We detail how these attacks are performed 
by adversaries. Genomic data is vulnerable to various types of privacy attacks. These attacks exploit statistical, compu-
tational, and AI-driven methods to extract sensitive genetic information. Table  1 summarizes these attacks.
Identity tracing attacks use quasi-identifiers such as age, sex, and location to re-identify individuals from de-identified 
genomic datasets. Techniques like genealogical triangulation and public record linkage enable adversaries to match 
genetic data with existing demographic information. This creates a significant privacy risk [5–8]. Also, inference attacks, 
including Attribute Disclosure and Membership Inference, allow attackers to infer sensitive phenotypic traits or deter -
mine an individual’s participation in a genomic study. They do this by analyzing allele frequencies or dataset summary 
statistics. Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) have been particularly susceptible to these attacks. Because of 
this, stricter access control measures are necessary [9 –12]. Completion attacks, also known as genome reconstruction 
attacks, leverage genetic similarities among family members to infer missing genotypic information. High-profile cases, 
such as the Golden State Killer investigation, show how forensic genealogy and public DNA databases can be exploited 
for identity reconstruction [2, 13, 14].
Furthermore, advancements in machine learning and Bayesian networks have introduced novel threats to genomic data 
security. Bayesian networks have been used to predict missing genomic markers and perform identity inference. This remains 
possible even when differential privacy protections are applied [15, 16]. AI-driven machine learning-based re-identification 
techniques weaken de-identification strategies. They use deep learning models to match anonymized genomic sequences 
to identified datasets [17, 18]. Additionally, adversarial attacks on genomic AI models manipulate input data to mislead 
predictive models. This compromises their accuracy in genomic classification tasks [19–21]. These attacks include white-box

As AI and cryptographic solutions evolve, a hybrid security approach is essential. It must integrate robust encryption, 
adversarially trained AI models, and privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks. These measures are necessary to 
safeguard genomic data against emerging threats.
3  Technical solutions to mitigate genetic attacks
Companies and laboratories are increasingly outsourcing genetic information to cloud services due to benefits such as 
computational resources and cost savings [22]. However, storing data on clouds makes it vulnerable to cyber-attacks, neces-
sitating strict access controls to ensure only authorized individuals can access the data. In addition, genomic technologies 
like sequencers, now capable of sequencing a whole genome in days, are often connected Internet of Things (IoT) devices. 
These devices are vulnerable to security threats due to their full internet connectivity and inherent limitations in processing, 
memory, and power. To mitigate genetic data attacks, several techniques are employed as summarized in Table 2. These

sections.title: 3.1 Data perturbation methods
sections.text:
To protect privacy when sharing de-identified data, perturbation methods such as data transformation, aggregation, obfus-
cation, and synthetic data generation can be used. Data transformation modifies the format or structure of data. A common 
method is k-anonymity, which ensures each quasi-identifier sequence (e.g., race, birth) appears at least k times in a dataset 
[26]. For example, ZIP codes can be generalized to larger regions by reducing a 5-digit ZIP code (e.g., 02139) to a 3-digit 
prefix (e.g., 021xx). Generalizing ZIP codes in this way groups individuals into broader geographic categories. This makes it 
more likely that each group contains at least k people who share the same quasi-identifiers (like birth date, gender, and the 
generalized ZIP code), which satisfies the privacy condition of k-anonymity. As a result, it becomes harder for an adversary 
to isolate and identify individuals based on detailed location information. This is particularly important because 5-digit ZIP 
codes, when combined with birth date and gender, can uniquely identify over 50% of U.S. residents [27]. This type of gener-
alization is a common technique to protect against identity tracing attacks that exploit quasi-identifiers.
Data aggregation summarizes data instead of revealing individual records. The Beacon Network, developed by the 
Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH), preserves privacy by responding to user queries with a simple “yes” or 
“no” as to whether a specific allele exists in a dataset, without exposing raw data [2]. This binary response format restricts 
direct access to individual-level information. In addition, privacy is further supported by methods such as query aggrega-
tion, rate limiting, and the potential integration of differential privacy, which together reduce the risk of re-identification 
through repeated or cross-referenced queries [2 ]. Data obfuscation adds noise to mask sensitive information. A key 
method is differential privacy, which limits membership inference attacks through a privacy budget. While effective, it 
must balance privacy and data utility. Combining differential privacy with cryptographic methods or using a weaker 
adversarial model can improve data usability [2]. An algorithm satisfies differential privacy if its output remains nearly the 
same with or without an individual’s data [28]. The privacy parameter /u1D700 (or /u1D716 ) controls privacy strength; lower values add 
more noise, enhancing privacy [28, 29]. Equation (1) defines the conditions for a mechanism to meet differential privacy.

Exponential mechanisms provide strong utility guarantees by quickly omitting lower-quality outcomes [31]. Dwork and 
Roth showed that the exponential mechanism ensures high utility by not significantly lowering the utility score of any 
returned element compared to the maximum score in the database [31].
DP mechanisms are proposed for genomics studies to provide privacy guarantees [32], but they do not consider data 
dependencies [33]. Data may be dependent due to social, behavioral, and genomic interactions [34, 35]. Adversaries could 
infer susceptibility to diseases using family genome correlations [36]. Researchers have shown that user dependencies 
can predict sensitive information from differentially private queries [34, 37].
3.2  Current machine learning methods for protecting genetic privacy and security
Machine learning has seen significant success in recent years and is now being applied in various fields, including bio -
informatics, medicine, and health care. Research has focused on using machine learning models to protect sensitive 
information from leakage.
3.2.1  Differentiable private stochastic gradient descent (DP‑SGD)
Zhang et al. [38] proposed the functional mechanism, a differential privacy technique designed for optimization-based 
analyses. This mechanism enforces /u1D700-differential privacy by perturbing the objective function of the optimization problem

sections.title: 3.2.2 Federated learning
sections.text:
A study proposed using federated learning (FL) to address challenges in sharing genomics data and handling large vol-
umes of data [41]. FL trains a machine learning model using data from multiple devices without distributing the data, 
addressing privacy, security, and access control issues. Figure 3 shows devices training models locally and sending them 
to a centralized server to create a global model. FL generates valuable insights from sensitive data, but additional safety 
mechanisms are needed. Aziz et al. used differential privacy and the exponential mechanism to protect genetic data 
privacy, creating private histograms and applying differential privacy after data dimension reduction [41].

Data-private collaborative learning (DPCL) enables model training across institutions without sharing patient data, 
unlike the Collaborative Data Sharing approach (CDS) [42]. Examples include Cyclic Institutional Incremental Learning 
(CIIL) and Institutional Incremental Learning (IIL), which are prone to “catastrophic forgetting” [43]. In IIL, each institution 
trains the model once before passing it to the next institution, while in CIIL, institutions can train more than once with a 
fixed number of training epochs [42]. Also, Sheller et al. showed that FL converges faster and performs better than CDS, 
CIIL, and IIL, with less bias due to aggregated results [42].
FL addresses privacy, data ownership, and technical concerns, encouraging multi-institutional collaborations and 
leading to accurate models for medical applications [42]. FL complies with HIPAA and GDPR but is vulnerable to privacy 
attacks like inference, reconstruction, and backdoors [44, 45]. Researchers should conduct privacy analysis and supple -
ment models with other privacy-preserving techniques [46, 47].

sections.title: 3.3 Cryptographic solutions
sections.text:
To address concerns related to outsourcing genomic data to untrusted cloud environments, unauthorized use beyond 
agreed research scopes, and potential privacy breaches, cryptographic techniques have been developed to safeguard 
genomic data and prevent privacy leakage. One widely studied approach is Homomorphic Encryption (HE), which enables 
computations on encrypted data without requiring decryption. This technique allows secure outsourcing of statistical

where m i represents a message, E and D are encryption and decryption schemes, and op and oe are operations on plain 
and encrypted messages, respectively. HE schemes are classified as partially HE (supporting only addition or multiplica-
tion), somewhat HE (allowing limited operations), and fully HE (enabling arbitrary computations on encrypted data).
Kim et al. [50] proposed an HE-based framework to protect genotype data during imputation. This allows computa-
tions to be performed securely without exposing sensitive genetic sequences. Additionally, Mahdi et al. [24] improved 
privacy-preserving genomic searches by using an encrypted Generalized Suffix Tree (GST). In this method, genomic data 
is encrypted before storage. Secure access is ensured through a cryptographic protocol. This framework, as shown in 
Figure 4, involves multiple entities, including hospitals, research institutions, and cloud servers. These entities manage 
encryption keys and enable secure queries using Garbled Circuit (GC) protocols [51].
Another cryptographic approach is Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMC). This method allows multiple parties to 
analyze genomic datasets together without exposing individual data points [2 ]. In SMC, sensitive genomic data is split 
into secret shares and distributed among multiple entities. No single entity has access to the complete data. Computation 
is carried out over these shares using cryptographic protocols such as additive secret sharing, Shamir’s secret sharing, 
or garbled circuits [52]. Each party performs operations only on its share of the data, and the intermediate results are 
combined at the end to reconstruct the final output. This approach ensures data privacy throughout the process. Many 
SMC implementations use homomorphic encryption and secret sharing to improve data security. GC-based techniques 
provide additional privacy protection [3, 53]. However, despite its privacy benefits, SMC has scalability issues. High com-
putation and communication costs make it impractical for large-scale genomic datasets.
To overcome some of these limitations, researchers have explored Secure Cryptographic Hardware (SCH) solutions. 
One example is Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX), which creates secure enclaves within CPUs to protect data dur -
ing computation [54, 55]. Unlike software-based encryption techniques, SCH provides hardware-enforced security. This 
ensures that genomic data remains protected even during processing. Chen et al. [56] introduced an SCH-based tech-
nique to securely outsource genetic testing to untrusted cloud environments. This makes SCH a scalable alternative for 
genomic privacy. However, SCH still has challenges. It struggles to handle large-scale genomic datasets due to limited 
memory capacity. It also has potential security vulnerabilities that need further investigation [3 ].
Apart from cryptographic encryption, Differential Privacy (DP) has been widely used to enhance genomic privacy, 
especially in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS). DP adds carefully calibrated noise to summary statistics, such 
as Minor Allele Frequencies (MAFs), chi-square ( x2 ) statistics, and P-values. This prevents adversaries from inferring indi-
vidual genomic data [9]. While DP helps reduce privacy risks, it often lowers data utility. To balance privacy and accuracy, 
researchers have explored relaxed DP models, such as Pufferfish Privacy [57], Bayesian Differential Privacy [58], and Rényi 
Differential Privacy (RDP) [59], which adjust adversarial assumptions or redefine sensitivity to improve usability while 
maintaining privacy as applicable to protecting against membership inference attacks [60].

sections.title: 3.4 Blockchain solution
sections.text:
Blockchain is a shared, immutable database that records and distributes digital information among authorized partici-
pants [61]. It has been considered for genomic data sharing while protecting privacy [62, 63]. Researchers have proposed 
using blockchain to securely share GWAS datasets or machine learning (ML) model parameters trained on genomics 
data [64]. Figure  6 illustrates how blockchain functions in genomics. Access to genomic data is controlled by multiple 
independent parties holding shares of a split encryption key [16]. The blockchain ensures immutable storage of indi-
viduals’ consent and data access requests [16]. Key features include user anonymity, access control, record auditability, 
and secure data analysis [62].
Grishin et al. [62] proposed pseudo-anonymous transactions using blockchain addresses for genetic testing. This 
method hides identity information and reduces the need for data de-identification. They also introduced delegated access 
control, where multiple independent organizations manage data access [62]. Blockchain further enables tamper-proof 
record-keeping by storing data access requests and user consent [ 62]. When an investigator requests access, encryp -
tion key holders read permissions from the blockchain, decrypt the data, and grant access if authorized [62]. This model 
supports secure computing by “bringing algorithms to the data, ” reducing exposure of sensitive information. Grishin 
et al. [62] recommended privacy-preserving technologies like homomorphic encryption (HE) and secure multiparty 
computation (SMC) to enhance security. Recent advances have made these technologies more practical and scalable 
for direct-to-consumer (DTC) genomics companies [65].

sections.title: 3.5 Synthetic data generation techniques
sections.text:
Researchers have proposed synthetic data generation to protect anonymity. Deep learning models like Generative 
Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) generate data that maintains the characteristics 
of the original data, reducing the risk of malicious inference [66]. However, synthetic data may not always guarantee 
privacy and utility. Oprisanu et al. [67] studied methods like Recombination model (Recomb), RBMs, GANs, WGANS, Rec-
RBM, and Rec-GAN, measuring their utility and privacy. The Recomb model on the HapMap dataset had the best utility 
but reduced privacy. No single method was best across all metrics and datasets, indicating further research is needed 
to achieve high privacy and utility. Likewise, Jordan et al. in [68] used differential privacy in GANs with the PATE-GAN 
framework, bounding the influence of individual samples to ensure privacy and improve performance. Their experiments 
showed the synthetic data was as useful as the original and outperformed other methods.

sections.title: 3.6 Access control solutions
sections.text:
Preventing unauthorized access is crucial for genomics privacy and security. The U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) 
and the Wellcome Trust Foundation mitigated attacks by moving demographic information and GWAS summary statis-
tics into controlled-access databases [69, 70]. Various access control models are used to prevent data breaches. Another 
model applicable in the context genomics privacy is using a trust-but-verify approach, recording and auditing transac -
tions to detect malicious activities [71]. A participant-based model grants original participants control over their data and 
manages access through a trusted agent [71]. Furthermore, the NIH prefers an authority-based access control solution 
over identity-based methods. This context-sensitive model recognizes the source of authority, grants minimal necessary 
privileges, and uses the Research Authorization Service (RAS) to verify identities and issue authorization tokens [72 ]. 
However, NIH’s reliance on commercial cloud storage, which uses identity-based solutions, poses security risks. More so, 
Mosca and colleagues highlight a significant concern indicating the genomic data protection through on controlled-
access databases might not be adequately shielded from unauthorized users [73].
3.7  Translating privacy‑preserving techniques into practice: real‑world genomic frameworks
The Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) is a worldwide group that creates technical and policy guidelines 
to support the safe and ethical sharing of genomic data. It aims to balance data access with privacy protection. To achieve 
this, GA4GH has developed a set of standards that enable collaboration while keeping sensitive genomic information 
secure. These standards use data masking, encryption, and access control to reduce privacy risks in research. Some key 
standards include the Beacon Project, which allows controlled data queries, and the Passport Standard, which supports 
secure authentication across different systems. Other initiatives, like CanDIG, enable privacy-focused data analysis, while 
DUOS automates decisions on data use. These efforts show that privacy-preserving methods can work in large-scale 
genomic data management [74–77].

sections.title: 3.7.1 GA4GH Beacon Project
sections.text:
The GA4GH Beacon Project helps researchers find genomic data while protecting privacy. It allows users to check if a 
specific allele is present. It gives a simple “yes” or “no” answer without revealing raw data. Beacons limit direct access to 
datasets and use query aggregation to lower the risk of identifying individuals. However, privacy risks still exist. If multiple 
Beacons are queried together, statistical methods could be used to infer sensitive information. To prevent this, stronger 
privacy techniques like differential privacy or threshold-based responses may be needed [74].

sections.title: 3.7.2 GA4GH passport standard
sections.text:
The GA4GH Passport Standard introduces a federated authentication and authorization model. It grants role-based 
access to genomic datasets using machine-readable “visas. ” These visas are individual assertions about a user’s roles or 
data access rights. They define user permissions and are encoded within JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). Both Passports and 
Visas are digitally signed using cryptographic algorithms such as Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA), Rivest-Shamir-Adleman

(RSA), and Elliptic Curve (EC) [78, 79]. By using these cryptographic schemes, the GA4GH Passport Standard ensures 
that user permissions are securely transmitted and verifiable across different systems in the genomics and health data-
sharing ecosystem. This approach improves interoperability and security. However, it still depends on centralized trust 
authorities, which could fail in multi-institutional collaborations. Also, verifying user credentials alone does not prevent 
unethical data use. This makes insider threat mitigation an ongoing challenge [75].

sections.title: 3.7.3 CanDIG federated data sharing
sections.text:
The CanDIG Federated Data Sharing platform is closely related to Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMC). It allows 
genomic analysis across institutions without revealing raw data (CanDIG Consortium, 2022). It ensures that institutions 
keep control over their datasets. This reduces the risks linked to centralized genomic repositories. However, SMC has 
major computational challenges. It requires high processing power and is complex to implement. This may limit its abil-
ity to handle large genomic studies. Federated querying helps protect raw data, but it does not fully eliminate the risk 
of inference attacks. Additional safeguards, like noise injection or differential privacy, are needed [76].

sections.title: 3.7.4 Data use ontology (DUO) system
sections.text:
The Data Use Ontology (DUO) system strengthens genomic privacy. It does this by enforcing policy-driven access restric-
tions (GA4GH Ethics and Policy Working Group, 2021). The DUO system employs structured Data Use Limitations (DULs) to 
automate access approvals. This ensures compliance with ethical and legal frameworks. This system reduces administra-
tive burdens. However, it relies on predefined policies. This reliance may lead to inflexibility when addressing emerging 
privacy risks. A more adaptive governance model could enhance its effectiveness in preventing unauthorized access [77].
Overall, these genomic privacy frameworks show how privacy-preserving techniques are applied in genomic research. 
They prove the feasibility of federated authentication, cryptographic protections, and policy-driven oversight. However, 
challenges remain in scalability, computational efficiency, and resistance to inference attacks. Future advancements 
should focus on hybrid cryptographic methods and adaptive privacy-preserving techniques. These improvements will 
help strengthen genomic data security.
4  Laws and policies related to genetic information

sections.title: 4.1 Current policies
sections.text:
The rapid expansion of genomics and data-sharing technologies challenges genetic privacy regulation. Public policies 
aim to balance individual privacy with societal benefits, but defining privacy in the digital era remains complex [ 81]. 
Below are key regulations governing genetic data protection.
4.1.1  Health insurance portability and accountability act (HIPAA)
HIPAA, enacted in 1996, regulates healthcare entities but excludes private companies [81]. Its privacy rule protects 
personal health data while allowing controlled use for public health [ 82]. The security rule mandates administrative, 
technical, and physical safeguards for electronic health information but excludes oral and written transmissions [82]. 
HIPAA permits data sharing without consent if de-identified using Safe Harbor or Expert Determination methods, which 
assess re-identification risks [83].

sections.title: 4.1.2 General data protection regulation (GDPR)
sections.text:
The GDPR enforces strict privacy controls on personal data, including genomic information, processed by organizations 
handling EU citizens’ data [84, 85]. It mandates data controllers to maintain security throughout data processing and 
ensures de-identified data remains irreversible [84]. Entities must adhere to seven principles: accountability, storage 
limitation, accuracy, data minimization, purpose limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and transparency [86].

4.1.3  Genetic information discrimination law and the genetic information privacy act
The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) provides limited protection against genetic discrimination. It 
mainly applies to employment and health insurance [87, 88]. It does not cover epigenome, microbiome, or metagenome 
data [25]. Some states, like California, have stronger protections under the Genetic Information Privacy Act (GIPA). This law 
defines genetic data broadly and requires explicit consent for testing and data sharing [25, 89]. Other states, including 
Virginia and Colorado, have passed similar privacy laws [89– 91]. Furthermore, GIPA requires direct-to-consumer (DTC) 
genetic testing companies to obtain consent before collecting, using, or sharing genetic data. Consumers have the right 
to revoke consent, delete data, and request account removal on platforms like 23andMe [23]. Additionally, GIPA requires 
a court order for law enforcement or third-party access to genetic data [23].

sections.title: 4.2 Surreptitious genetic testing (SGT)
sections.text:
SGT refers to collecting and analyzing DNA without a person’s knowledge or consent. This raises ethical and legal con-
cerns. No federal law explicitly bans SGT, but some states have restrictions with different penalties [81, 92, 93]. GINA and 
the Affordable Care Act (ACA) provide limited protections. They apply only to employment and health insurance [81 ]. 
DTC companies have created internal policies that require users to verify ownership or get consent before submitting 
genetic samples. However, enforcement is inconsistent. A major case involving the Golden State Killer highlighted these 
concerns. Investigators used a public genealogy database (GEDMatch) and secretly collected DNA from a discarded tis-
sue and a car door handle [81]. Police obtained a court order for genetic testing, but they searched GEDMatch without 
prior approval. This raised privacy concerns. Most jurisdictions do not require warrants for surreptitious DNA collection. 
As a result, individuals remain vulnerable to forensic genetic surveillance [94].
5  Addressing genomics data privacy and security issues
In this section, we summarize current challenges and provide recommendations for securing genomics data.
5.1  Challenging problems in genomic data privacy and security
The rapid growth of genomic data sharing has increased privacy and security risks. This has created a need for strong 
cryptographic and privacy-preserving techniques. Traditional methods like homomorphic encryption (HE), secure multi-
party computation (SMC), and federated learning (FL) provide security guarantees. However, they also cause computa-
tional inefficiencies. AI-driven attacks and the risk of quantum decryption add more challenges. To address these issues, 
genomic privacy frameworks must be redesigned. They should include AI-resilient security mechanisms and quantum-
resistant cryptographic methods.
5.1.1  Trade‑offs in cryptographic security and computational efficiency for genomic data protection
Genomic data encryption has always struggled to balance privacy, efficiency, and usability. Techniques like HE and SMC 
provide strong security. They allow computations on encrypted data without revealing sensitive information. However, 
these methods create high computational overhead, making them impractical for large-scale genomic analysis and 
real-time applications [2 , 3, 95]. In contrast, lighter cryptographic methods like Secure Hybrid Rivest-Shamir-Adleman 
(SHRSA) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are more efficient. They are widely used for secure genomic data transmis-
sion [96, 97]. For example, Barmana and Saha in [97] proposed a DNA Encoded Elliptic Curve Cryptography System for 
IoT security. However, the security of these cryptographic methods depends on the difficulty of certain mathematical 
problems. RSA relies on integer factorization, while ECC is based on the discrete logarithm problem. These problems 
are too complex for classical computers but can be solved efficiently using Shor’s algorithm on a quantum computer 
[98, 99]. This growing vulnerability has increased interest in quantum-resistant cryptographic approaches, which are 
discussed further in Section 5.2. Additionally, privacy-enhancing techniques like Differentiable Private Stochastic Gradi-
ent Descent (DP-SGD) and federated learning (FL), detailed in Section 3.2, have been proposed for genomic security [38, 
39, 41]. However, these methods face new risks from AI-driven attacks. These attacks use machine learning models to 
infer sensitive genomic information.
